title: Listen, Do Not Copy: Internalizing Audio-Grounded Scaffold Contextfor Robust Omni-Model Speech Understanding

paper.title: Listen, Do Not Copy: Internalizing Audio-Grounded Scaffold Context for Robust Omni-Model Speech Understanding
paper.abstract: Abstract Omni models transcribe clean, single-speaker speech well, but their accuracy drops sharply when speakers overlap and the scene is noisy, exactly where knowing who said what matters most. A natural fix is a short scene description. We show why this is risky: answer-bearing text lets the model copy instead of listen, so the score rises although nothing has been heard; a silent test exposes this shortcut at once. We call this failure mode perception bypass and address it with Audio-Grounded Scaffold Context (AGSC) . AGSC links three steps: first, we build clues from audio to guide listening without giving the answer; second, answer-overlap and silence tests probe them for leakage and audio dependence; finally, those clues scaffold training but vanish at test time, yielding no-clue capability. Across three heterogeneous Omni models, training on AGSC lowers no-clue capped mean permutation word error rate (mpWER) on overlapping, noisy speech from 25 % 25\% – 71 % 71\% to 9 % 9\% – 15 % 15\% . For streaming control, we formulate a joint GDPO task in which the model learns when to use a clue and how to produce a speaker-attributed transcript from separately normalized format, gate, and transcript rewards. After internalization, AGSC adds almost no inference overhead.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Imagine a meeting recording in which two people briefly speak at once over the hum of an air conditioner. An Omni model is a multimodal large language model that handles text, images, audio, and video in one backbone ( Xu et al. 2025 ; Cui et al. 2026 ; Inclusion AI et al. 2025b ) . It may transcribe the clean parts well and then fail at the overlap: it merges two voices, drops a speaker, or treats noise as words. These conditions are common in meetings, call centers, in-car assistants, and interviews, where knowing who said what is hardest and most useful. Textual scene descriptions seem like a natural aid when audio is unclear. We tried the most direct version and supplied a full transcript as context. The mean accuracy of three Omni models rose from about 53 % 53\% to 94 % 94\% . The jump was too good to be true. On the primary-transcript task, the two stronger models copied a wrong contextual answer 94 % 94\% – 99.8 % 99.8\% of the time; the weakest copied it 47 % 47\% of the time. With silence in place of audio, all three still reached 100 % 100\% primary-transcript accuracy. The high score measured copying, not better listening. We call this failure mode perception bypass and turn it into a pass-or-fail test for context quality. This observation is our starting point. We hypothesize that Omni models already have useful acoustic capabilities that remain underused in complex scenes. Audio-Grounded Scaffold Context (AGSC) has two goals: draw out those capabilities and keep text from mimicking better listening. Its clues give only limited scene structure, and a silent-audio control checks whether the clue alone can still succeed without the audio signal. Figure 1: Overview. (a) Answer-bearing context inflates scores by copying. (b) AGSC provides limited-content scaffold clues with three safeguards. (c) After supervised training, capped mean permutation word error rate (mpWER) stays lower when the clue is removed. The silent test is an aggregate control; we use the no-clue gain as operational evidence of internalization . We test this idea with AGSC (Figure 1 ). Instead of telling the model what was said, AGSC supplies three kinds of scaffolding: target-speaker activity, scene noise level, and partial, shuffled words. Each clue should guide listening, not become a text-only solution. To limit or expose context-only shortcuts, we use three safeguards: an audio-first instruction , an answer-overlap screen , and a silent-audio control . Standard tools build the clues from raw audio. We use two training paths so the learned behavior is not tied to a fixed test-time prompt. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) mixes scaffolded and plain inputs; after training, we remove clues and treat the retained no-clue gain as a behavioral definition of internalization . Group reward-decoupled normalization policy optimization (GDPO) ( Liu et al. 2026 ) handles streaming control with separate rewards for output format, gate decisions, and transcript quality. Gate-only training learns whether and when to use a clue; full-chain training learns the gate and speaker-attributed transcript jointly. Both paths update low-rank adapters. We make three contributions. (1) We identify perception bypass and turn silent audio into a behavioral design test for context. (2) We introduce AGSC (an automatic synthesis pipeline) and Context-Speech Bench (CSB) , which covers overlap, noise, meetings, streaming clues, and gating. (3) We show internalization: supervised training improves no-clue transcription, and one GDPO stage jointly trains gate and transcript outputs with streaming clues from 160 160 streams. We report silent-audio controls beside the context results; following acceptance, we will open-source the AGSC code, benchmark manifests, and result evidence to support reproducibility and advance community research.

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.text: Audio-language models join an audio encoder with a large language model. They range from Qwen-Audio ( Chu et al. 2023 ) and SALMONN ( Tang et al. 2024 ) to Omni systems that understand and generate several modalities ( Xu et al. 2025 ; Cui et al. 2026 ; Inclusion AI et al. 2025a ; Inclusion AI et al. 2025b ) . Speaker-attributed transcription remains difficult under overlap and noise ( Kanda et al. 2020 ; Cornell et al. 2024 ) . AIR-Bench, MMAU, and Dynamic-SUPERB mainly test broad listening and reasoning ability ( Yang et al. 2024 ; Sakshi et al. 2025 ; Huang et al. 2024 ) . They do not directly test whether textual context leaks the answer. We add this control to Qwen3-Omni, MiniCPM-o, and Ming-flash-omni (henceforth Qwen3, MiniCPM, and Ming). The classical route chains diarization ( Bredin 2023 ) , voice activity detection ( Silero Team 2024 ) , automatic speech recognition (ASR) ( Radford et al. 2023 ) , and sometimes separation ( Subakan et al. 2021 ) ; early errors can spread. A second route trains one model to emit several speakers ( Kanda et al. 2020 ) , uses speaker profiles ( Medennikov et al. 2020 ) , or targets distant meetings ( Cornell et al. 2024 ) . We train low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules on the attention projections and leave the pretrained weights unchanged ( Hu et al. 2022 ) . We reuse the front-end tools in a different role: they produce clues that the model must still check against audio, not answers it can copy. We keep a front-end component only when measurements show that it helps. Our focus is context design and parameter-efficient adaptation of Omni models, not a separate transcription cascade. Retrieval-augmented generation adds text from an external memory ( Lewis et al. 2020 ) , while chain-of-thought prompting exposes intermediate reasoning steps ( Wei et al. 2022 ) . Contextual biasing gives a recognizer trusted word lists, such as contact names ( Pundak et al. 2018 ) . Our candidate words are different: they are automatic, possibly wrong, partial, and shuffled. Text-only systems can also rewrite recognition or diarization outputs ( Chen et al. 2023 ; Wang et al. 2024 ) , but they cannot use the audio to correct a fluent but wrong draft. AGSC instead keeps audio as the source of the answer and limits context to partial clues that the model must check against the signal. Perception bypass is a form of shortcut learning ( Geirhos et al. 2020 ) . Our silent test has a role similar to language-prior controls used to rebalance visual question answering datasets ( Goyal et al. 2017 ) . Related failures also occur in vision-language and audio-video models ( Deng et al. 2025 ; Nishimura et al. 2024 ; Leng et al. 2025 ) . Recent work shows that large audio models can answer from text alone and uses that signal to split training data ( He et al. 2026 ) . We instead use silence as a design criterion and an empirical control: context should fail without audio. Context distillation moves the benefit of instructions or scratchpads into model weights ( Snell et al. 2022 ) . We ask a related question: does clue-conditioned training improve no-clue evaluation, and can a model learn when a clue would be useful? Interference-Resilient Adaptive Fusion (IRAF) studies a related problem in full-duplex dialogue, where an interfering speaker enters the user microphone ( Zhong et al. 2026 ) . It predicts input reliability and suppresses an unreliable signal. Both IRAF and our method use a learned gate, but at different points. IRAF reduces interference before fusion; we keep every speaker and gate a limited-content text clue. Its continuous gate provides a useful comparison with our discrete clue gate.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: AGSC has three linked steps: it synthesizes answer-incomplete clues from audio, screens them for direct answer exposure and audio dependence, and uses them as removable training scaffolds. A separate GDPO study learns a joint gate-plus-transcript output for streaming control.

sections.heading: Problem and Perception Bypass
sections.text: Given an audio clip a a with K K speakers, the model must output one line per speaker. Let y = ( y 1 , … , y K ) y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{K}) be the gold transcriptions and y ^ \hat{y} the predicted lines. We score outputs with mean permutation word error rate (mpWER), a speaker-averaged variant of concatenated minimum-permutation word error rate (cpWER) ( Watanabe et al. 2020 ) . It is the equally weighted mean of per-speaker word error rates (WER) under the best speaker permutation (lower is better): mpWER ⁡ ( y , y ^ ) = min ρ ∈ S K ⁡ 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K ED ⁡ ( y k , y ^ ρ ⁡ ( k ) ) | y k | \mathrm{mpWER}(y,\hat{y})=\min_{\rho\in S_{K}}\ \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\mathrm{ED}\big(y_{k},\hat{y}_{\rho(k)}\big)}{|y_{k}|} (1) In Equation ( 1 ), ρ ∈ S K \rho\in S_{K} assigns lines to reference speakers, ED \mathrm{ED} is word-level edit distance, and | y k | |y_{k}| is reference length. Missing output lines are padded as empty. For this two-speaker benchmark, including streaming evaluation, we score only the first two output lines. Let c c be a textual context. We seek a context whose gain depends on a a , not on c c alone. An overly informative c c can make a a irrelevant; this is perception bypass. The introduction showed that a transcript-bearing context inflates accuracy by copying: the answer is a copyable substring, wrong labels are copied, and silent audio still scores perfectly. We turn this finding into a design criterion. For model M M , a clue c c is desirable for sample ( a , y ) (a,y) only when it cannot solve the sample without audio: mpWER ⁡ ( y , M ⁡ ( a ∅ , c ) ) ≥ η \mathrm{mpWER}\big(y,\,M(a_{\varnothing},c)\big)\ \geq\ \eta (2) where a ∅ a_{\varnothing} is a silent track of the same length as a a . We set η = 1 \eta=1 (an mpWER of at least 1 1 ) for transcription; for classification probes, we report accuracy and use chance level as the analogous boundary. Equation ( 2 ) states the desired sample-level property. At evaluation, we apply the same idea at the aggregate level by measuring performance after the audio is silenced. This is an empirical control, not a proof that every shortcut is absent.

sections.heading: AGSC: Clues, Not Answers
sections.text: This rule leads directly to a simple design principle: a clue may point and narrow, but it must not disclose the answer. AGSC applies this principle to each acoustic scene. For overlap, AGSC provides a time window for each speaker, such as target active 0.00–3.85 s, female , but no words. For single-speaker noise, it provides a coarse noise level, speech regions, and a partial, shuffled word list. We keep about two thirds of the candidate words and remove exact answers such as digits. For overlap plus noise, a separator produces a rough draft for each voice. AGSC keeps half of the content words, adds up to four distractors from other recordings, removes duplicates, and shuffles the result. It never shows the full draft. Figure 1 (b) shows this format. Missing words, distractors, and lost word order reduce directly copyable content. The clue type matches the uncertainty. A time window addresses who and when ; coarse attributes describe the listening condition; and a lossy word set narrows lexical alternatives. Removing sentence order, completeness, and exact-value tokens keeps the clue directional rather than answer-like. An overlap-plus-noise clue therefore labels its candidates as partial, shuffled, and possibly wrong, omits much of the draft, and never presents a complete sentence. Three safeguards limit or expose shortcuts. The audio-first instruction marks every clue as automatic and fallible. The answer-overlap screen rejects a directly copyable answer string, while the silent-audio control tests whether the remaining clue can still replace sound. Clean audio does not need a clue, so a gate adds one only for detected overlap or low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The gate handles a separate risk: a non-answer clue can still distract a segment that needs no help.

sections.heading: Automatic Synthesis Pipeline
sections.text: The automatic pipeline turns raw audio into AGSC. It diarizes speakers ( Bredin 2023 ) , runs segment ASR to obtain candidate words, and detects overlap, speech regions ( Silero Team 2024 ) , and a coarse SNR level. For overlap plus noise, SepFormer separates the voices ( Subakan et al. 2021 ) ; per-speaker ASR then supplies words for shuffling. The gate decides whether to add a clue, and the exporter records the clue with a confidence tag. Each component must earn its place through measurement. We select the diarizer with lower diarization error rate (DER, 0.22 0.22 versus 0.47 0.47 ) and remove an acoustic-scene tagger with only 29 % 29\% accuracy. SNR is useful only as a coarse level: that level is correct 79 % 79\% of the time, although the point estimate has 9.9 9.9 dB mean error. On twelve evaluation recordings, the full pipeline reaches DER 0.15 0.15 , finds the correct speaker count for 83 % 83\% of clips, and obtains draft character error rate (CER) 0.20 0.20 . The confidence tag indicates how much the model should trust the front end rather than presenting an uncertain clue as ground truth.

sections.heading: Experiments
sections.text: We test three Omni models: Qwen3-Omni 30B ( Xu et al. 2025 ) , MiniCPM-o 4.5 (9B) ( Cui et al. 2026 ) , and Ming-flash-omni 2.0, a 100B-total, 6.1B-active-per-token mixture-of-experts model ( Inclusion AI et al. 2025b ) . CSB covers overlap, noise, meetings, streaming clue maturity, and gating. Its English speech comes from LibriSpeech and SparseLibriMix2 ( Panayotov et al. 2015 ; Cosentino et al. 2020 ) ; Mandarin comes from AISHELL-3 mixes ( Shi et al. 2021 ) ; noise comes from WHAM and the Music, Speech, and Noise (MUSAN) corpus ( Wichern et al. 2019 ; Snyder et al. 2015 ) ; and meetings come from the Augmented Multi-party Interaction (AMI) Meeting Corpus ( Carletta et al. 2006 ) . Gold answers and predicted clues are stored separately. CSB contains 13,255 13{,}255 training and 1,525 1{,}525 evaluation samples. It also has dedicated splits for gate-only reinforcement ( 120 120 streams; 240 240 paired windows), full-chain reinforcement ( 160 160 streams), clue maturity ( 385 385 prefix clues), and real-time gating ( 30 30 streams). The supplement gives the split table and construction details. We report mpWER, Mandarin CER, and gating F 1 (the harmonic mean of precision and recall). For each hardest-third summary, we select the subset once from the pre-training no-clue baseline and reuse it across conditions; these summaries are descriptive. The supervised and full-chain results cap the mpWER of each sample at 1 1 before averaging, while streaming diagnostics keep their recorded raw means. We report the available 95 % 95\% confidence intervals (CIs) for the full-set comparisons. The experiments follow four questions: does answer-bearing context replace listening; does scaffold-conditioned training improve transcription after the clue is removed; how does clue utility change with prefix maturity; and can reinforcement learning train the gate and full chain? A targeted AMI case between the first two questions illustrates how a wordless clue can guide target selection. This order separates shortcut detection, no-clue transfer, streaming utility, and learned control. The first question is whether perception bypass occurs (Table 1 ). The answer is clear. On the primary-transcript task, blind-copy rates reach 99.8 % 99.8\% with a wrong answer in context, and accuracy remains 100 % 100\% on silent audio. The inflated scores therefore measure copying. Ming copies less often ( 47 % 47\% ) mainly because it fails to follow the answer format, not because it listens better. All three models fail this control. By contrast, in the gated-AGSC silence control on the transcription and speaker-counting probes, the aggregate task score is 0 % 0\% when audio is replaced by silence but the original clue is kept. This is consistent with less context-only copying on these probes. Model No context +Answer Blind-copy Qwen3 65.6 93.3 94.2 MiniCPM 53.4 96.8 99.8 Ming 40.1 91.1 47.0 Table 1: Perception bypass. The first two columns are composite task scores (%); blind-copy is measured on the primary-transcript task under a wrong contextual answer. The copied answers show that the inflated score does not establish better listening. Before the training studies, we inspect a target-selection case on real AMI meetings. The unclued Qwen3 output can include speech beyond the target, consistent with target-location ambiguity. A predicted time window contains no transcript words; it narrows where to listen while leaving word recovery to audio. This illustrates the intended division of labor, not a claim of uniform test-time gain. This case also shows why a clue must match the scene. A time window addresses who and when ; under noise, partial and shuffled candidates narrow lexical uncertainty without becoming a second transcript. The three evaluations therefore answer different questions: no-clue transcription asks what remains after scaffold-conditioned training; the prefix study asks when a runtime clue becomes useful while the heard audio stays fixed; and joint training asks whether the learned gate-plus-transcript output is accurate. The second question is whether the post-training skill persists without a clue. Performance improves after AGSC fine-tuning even with no clue at test time on the 150 150 -sample overlap-plus-noise evaluation split (Figure 3 , Table 2 ). On this split, mpWER falls from 25 % 25\% – 71 % 71\% to 9 % 9\% – 15 % 15\% . On the hardest-third summaries, it falls from 50 % 50\% – 96 % 96\% to 13 % 13\% – 17 % 17\% . We use this persistence after clue removal as operational evidence of internalization. The weaker models gain more: Ming drops by 56 56 points, MiniCPM by 52 52 , and Qwen3 by 16 16 . All three end in a narrow 9 9 – 15 15 band. The same pattern holds for overlap without added noise, where mpWER falls from 26.6 26.6 , 64.1 64.1 , and 68.3 68.3 to 8.4 8.4 , 14.9 14.9 , and 7.9 7.9 for Qwen3, MiniCPM, and Ming, respectively. The effect is therefore not tied to one test condition. For MiniCPM, an always-on test-time clue after training lags the no-clue result ( 22.5 22.5 versus 14.0 14.0 ). During training, clues arrive only through the gate, so the model sees them only for selected segments. Adding one unconditionally at test time therefore changes the input distribution and can hurt accuracy. sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: Our hypothesis is simple: some complex-scene failures reflect an underused capability, not an absent one. AGSC tries to draw out that capability without turning its clues into textual shortcuts. During SFT, an incomplete target window, condition tag, or candidate list acts as a temporary trigger. We call the lower error that remains after removing the trigger retained activation . Answer-overlap screening limits copying; the silent-audio control measures performance after silencing the audio. Each check answers a different question: context-on evaluation asks whether a clue helps; silence asks whether it can replace audio; no-clue evaluation asks whether behavior persists after scaffold removal; and streaming metrics ask whether assistance is timed correctly. No check substitutes for another. We use internalization for post-training persistence without clues. SFT targets persistence after scaffold removal; GDPO separates gate-only timing from full-chain gate-plus-transcript training under separately normalized rewards. How useful a clue is depends on the scene and on how much prefix audio was available to build it. A wordless window can narrow target location, while Figure 4 shows non-monotonic, model-specific changes as prefix evidence grows. Table 2 also shows that an unconditional clue after training need not beat the no-clue path. There is no universal prompt. Our predefined templates match clue type to the diagnosed ambiguity, and the gate limits when a clue enters. Together, the results separate what persists without runtime help (no-clue mpWER), when a clue should enter (gate metrics), and transcript accuracy under joint training (full-chain mpWER). Runtime clues remain in the streaming path, keeping assistance optional and failures visible.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This paper turns a tempting shortcut into a design principle. Answer-bearing context can let a model score without listening; we call this perception bypass and expose it by silencing audio. That test anchors three contributions: AGSC uses answer-incomplete scaffolds to guide listening while limiting direct copying; CSB evaluates them with explicit shortcut controls; and internalization is judged by whether gains persist after clues are removed. After SFT, no-clue capped mean mpWER on overlap plus noise falls from 25 % 25\% – 71 % 71\% to 9 % 9\% – 15 % 15\% , providing operational evidence of internalization. For streaming, gate-only GDPO learns whether and when to use a clue; full-chain GDPO jointly trains the gate and speaker-attributed transcript. Future work will extend scene-matched clues to new scene types and test the learned gate under domain shift. The deeper principle is simple: context should scaffold perception, not replace it.

A natural fix is a short scene description. We show why this is risky: answer-bearing text lets the model copy instead of listen, so the score rises although nothing has been heard; a silent test exposes this shortcut at once. We call this failure mode perception bypass and address it with Audio-Grounded Scaffold Context (AGSC) . AGSC links three steps: first, we build clues from audio to guide listening without giving the answer; second, answer-overlap and silence tests probe them for leakage and audio dependence; finally, those clues scaffold training but vanish at test time, yielding no-clue capability. Across three heterogeneous Omni models, training on AGSC lowers no-clue capped mean permutation word error rate (mpWER) on overlapping, noisy speech from 25 % 25\% – 71 % 71\% to 9 % 9\% – 15 % 15\% . For streaming control, we formulate a joint GDPO task in which the model learns when to use a clue and how to produce a speaker-attributed transcript from separately normalized format, gate, and transcript rewards. After internalization, AGSC adds almost no inference overhead. 1 AI Thrust, Information Hub, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) 2 Token Foundry, Alibaba Group avrillliu@hkust-gz.edu.cn Introduction Imagine a meeting recording in which two people briefly speak at once over the hum of an air conditioner. An Omni model is a multimodal large language model that handles text, images, audio, and video in one backbone ( Xu et al. 2025 ; Cui et al. 2026 ; Inclusion AI et al. 2025b ) . It may transcribe the clean parts well and then fail at the overlap: it merges two voices, drops a speaker, or treats noise as words. These conditions are common in meetings, call centers, in-car assistants, and interviews, where knowing who said what is hardest and most useful. Textual scene descriptions seem like a natural aid when audio is unclear. We tried the most direct version and supplied a full transcript as context. The mean accuracy of three Omni models rose from about 53 % 53\% to 94 % 94\% . The jump was too good to be true. On the primary-transcript task, the two stronger models copied a wrong contextual answer 94 % 94\% – 99.8 % 99.8\% of the time; the weakest copied it 47 % 47\% of the time. With silence in place of audio, all three still reached 100 % 100\% primary-transcript accuracy. The high score measured copying, not better listening. We call this failure mode perception bypass and turn it into a pass-or-fail test for context quality. This observation is our starting point. We hypothesize that Omni models already have useful acoustic capabilities that remain underused in complex scenes. Audio-Grounded Scaffold Context (AGSC) has two goals: draw out those capabilities and keep text from mimicking better listening. Its clues give only limited scene structure, and a silent-audio control checks whether the clue alone can still succeed without the audio signal. Figure 1: Overview. (a) Answer-bearing context inflates scores by copying. (b) AGSC provides limited-content scaffold clues with three safeguards. (c) After supervised training, capped mean permutation word error rate (mpWER) stays lower when the clue is removed. The silent test is an aggregate control; we use the no-clue gain as operational evidence of internalization . We test this idea with AGSC (Figure 1 ). Instead of telling the model what was said, AGSC supplies three kinds of scaffolding: target-speaker activity, scene noise level, and partial, shuffled words. Each clue should guide listening, not become a text-only solution. To limit or expose context-only shortcuts, we use three safeguards: an audio-first instruction , an answer-overlap screen , and a silent-audio control . Standard tools build the clues from raw audio. We use two training paths so the learned behavior is not tied to a fixed test-time prompt. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) mixes scaffolded and plain inputs; after training, we remove clues and treat the retained no-clue gain as a behavioral definition of internalization . Group reward-decoupled normalization policy optimization (GDPO) ( Liu et al. 2026 ) handles streaming control with separate rewards for output format, gate decisions, and transcript quality. Gate-only training learns whether and when to use a clue; full-chain training learns the gate and speaker-attributed transcript jointly. Both paths update low-rank adapters. We make three contributions. (1) We identify perception bypass and turn silent audio into a behavioral design test for context. (2) We introduce AGSC (an automatic synthesis pipeline) and Context-Speech Bench (CSB) , which covers overlap, noise, meetings, streaming clues, and gating. (3) We show internalization: supervised training improves no-clue transcription, and one GDPO stage jointly trains gate and transcript outputs with streaming clues from 160 160 streams. We report silent-audio controls beside the context results; following acceptance, we will open-source the AGSC code, benchmark manifests, and result evidence to support reproducibility and advance community research. Related Work Audio-language models join an audio encoder with a large language model. They range from Qwen-Audio ( Chu et al. 2023 ) and SALMONN ( Tang et al. 2024 ) to Omni systems that understand and generate several modalities ( Xu et al. 2025 ; Cui et al. 2026 ; Inclusion AI et al. 2025a ; Inclusion AI et al. 2025b ) . Speaker-attributed transcription remains difficult under overlap and noise ( Kanda et al. 2020 ; Cornell et al. 2024 ) . AIR-Bench, MMAU, and Dynamic-SUPERB mainly test broad listening and reasoning ability ( Yang et al. 2024 ; Sakshi et al. 2025 ; Huang et al. 2024 ) . They do not directly test whether textual context leaks the answer. We add this control to Qwen3-Omni, MiniCPM-o, and Ming-flash-omni (henceforth Qwen3, MiniCPM, and Ming). The classical route chains diarization ( Bredin 2023 ) , voice activity detection ( Silero Team 2024 ) , automatic speech recognition (ASR) ( Radford et al. 2023 ) , and sometimes separation ( Subakan et al. 2021 ) ; early errors can spread. A second route trains one model to emit several speakers ( Kanda et al. 2020 ) , uses speaker profiles ( Medennikov et al. 2020 ) , or targets distant meetings ( Cornell et al. 2024 ) . We train low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules on the attention projections and leave the pretrained weights unchanged ( Hu et al. 2022 ) . We reuse the front-end tools in a different role: they produce clues that the model must still check against audio, not answers it can copy. We keep a front-end component only when measurements show that it helps. Our focus is context design and parameter-efficient adaptation of Omni models, not a separate transcription cascade. Retrieval-augmented generation adds text from an external memory ( Lewis et al. 2020 ) , while chain-of-thought prompting exposes intermediate reasoning steps ( Wei et al. 2022 ) . Contextual biasing gives a recognizer trusted word lists, such as contact names ( Pundak et al. 2018 ) . Our candidate words are different: they are automatic, possibly wrong, partial, and shuffled. Text-only systems can also rewrite recognition or diarization outputs ( Chen et al. 2023 ; Wang et al. 2024 ) , but they cannot use the audio to correct a fluent but wrong draft. AGSC instead keeps audio as the source of the answer and limits context to partial clues that the model must check against the signal. Perception bypass is a form of shortcut learning ( Geirhos et al. 2020 ) . Our silent test has a role similar to language-prior controls used to rebalance visual question answering datasets ( Goyal et al. 2017 ) . Related failures also occur in vision-language and audio-video models ( Deng et al. 2025 ; Nishimura et al. 2024 ; Leng et al. 2025 ) . Recent work shows that large audio models can answer from text alone and uses that signal to split training data ( He et al. 2026 ) . We instead use silence as a design criterion and an empirical control: context should fail without audio. Context distillation moves the benefit of instructions or scratchpads into model weights ( Snell et al. 2022 ) . We ask a related question: does clue-conditioned training improve no-clue evaluation, and can a model learn when a clue would be useful? Interference-Resilient Adaptive Fusion (IRAF) studies a related problem in full-duplex dialogue, where an interfering speaker enters the user microphone ( Zhong et al. 2026 ) . It predicts input reliability and suppresses an unreliable signal. Both IRAF and our method use a learned gate, but at different points. IRAF reduces interference before fusion; we keep every speaker and gate a limited-content text clue. Its continuous gate provides a useful comparison with our discrete clue gate. Method AGSC has three linked steps: it synthesizes answer-incomplete clues from audio, screens them for direct answer exposure and audio dependence, and uses them as removable training scaffolds. A separate GDPO study learns a joint gate-plus-transcript output for streaming control. Problem and Perception Bypass Given an audio clip a a with K K speakers, the model must output one line per speaker. Let y = ( y 1 , … , y K ) y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{K}) be the gold transcriptions and y ^ \hat{y} the predicted lines. We score outputs with mean permutation word error rate (mpWER), a speaker-averaged variant of concatenated minimum-permutation word error rate (cpWER) ( Watanabe et al. 2020 ) . AGSC: Clues, Not Answers This rule leads directly to a simple design principle: a clue may point and narrow, but it must not disclose the answer. AGSC applies this principle to each acoustic scene. For overlap, AGSC provides a time window for each speaker, such as target active 0.00–3.85 s, female , but no words. For single-speaker noise, it provides a coarse noise level, speech regions, and a partial, shuffled word list. We keep about two thirds of the candidate words and remove exact answers such as digits. For overlap plus noise, a separator produces a rough draft for each voice. AGSC keeps half of the content words, adds up to four distractors from other recordings, removes duplicates, and shuffles the result. It never shows the full draft. Figure 1 (b) shows this format. Missing words, distractors, and lost word order reduce directly copyable content. The clue type matches the uncertainty. A time window addresses who and when ; coarse attributes describe the listening condition; and a lossy word set narrows lexical alternatives. Removing sentence order, completeness, and exact-value tokens keeps the clue directional rather than answer-like. An overlap-plus-noise clue therefore labels its candidates as partial, shuffled, and possibly wrong, omits much of the draft, and never presents a complete sentence. Three safeguards limit or expose shortcuts. The audio-first instruction marks every clue as automatic and fallible. The answer-overlap screen rejects a directly copyable answer string, while the silent-audio control tests whether the remaining clue can still replace sound. Clean audio does not need a clue, so a gate adds one only for detected overlap or low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The gate handles a separate risk: a non-answer clue can still distract a segment that needs no help. Automatic Synthesis Pipeline The automatic pipeline turns raw audio into AGSC. It diarizes speakers ( Bredin 2023 ) , runs segment ASR to obtain candidate words, and detects overlap, speech regions ( Silero Team 2024 ) , and a coarse SNR level. For overlap plus noise, SepFormer separates the voices ( Subakan et al. 2021 ) ; per-speaker ASR then supplies words for shuffling. The gate decides whether to add a clue, and the exporter records the clue with a confidence tag. Each component must earn its place through measurement. We select the diarizer with lower diarization error rate (DER, 0.22 0.22 versus 0.47 0.47 ) and remove an acoustic-scene tagger with only 29 % 29\% accuracy. SNR is useful only as a coarse level: that level is correct 79 % 79\% of the time, although the point estimate has 9.9 9.9 dB mean error. On twelve evaluation recordings, the full pipeline reaches DER 0.15 0.15 , finds the correct speaker count for 83 % 83\% of clips, and obtains draft character error rate (CER) 0.20 0.20 . The confidence tag indicates how much the model should trust the front end rather than presenting an uncertain clue as ground truth. Discussion Our hypothesis is simple: some complex-scene failures reflect an underused capability, not an absent one. AGSC tries to draw out that capability without turning its clues into textual shortcuts. During SFT, an incomplete target window, condition tag, or candidate list acts as a temporary trigger. We call the lower error that remains after removing the trigger retained activation . Answer-overlap screening limits copying; the silent-audio control measures performance after silencing the audio. Each check answers a different question: context-on evaluation asks whether a clue helps; silence asks whether it can replace audio; no-clue evaluation asks whether behavior persists after scaffold removal; and streaming metrics ask whether assistance is timed correctly. No check substitutes for another. We use internalization for post-training persistence without clues. SFT targets persistence after scaffold removal; GDPO separates gate-only timing from full-chain gate-plus-transcript training under separately normalized rewards. How useful a clue is depends on the scene and on how much prefix audio was available to build it. A wordless window can narrow target location, while Figure 4 shows non-monotonic, model-specific changes as prefix evidence grows. Table 2 also shows that an unconditional clue after training need not beat the no-clue path. There is no universal prompt. Our predefined templates match clue type to the diagnosed ambiguity, and the gate limits when a clue enters. Together, the results separate what persists without runtime help (no-clue mpWER), when a clue should enter (gate metrics), and transcript accuracy under joint training (full-chain mpWER). Runtime clues remain in the streaming path, keeping assistance optional and failures visible. Conclusion This paper turns a tempting shortcut into a design principle. Answer-bearing context can let a model score without listening; we call this perception bypass and expose it by silencing audio. That test anchors three contributions: AGSC uses answer-incomplete scaffolds to guide listening while limiting direct copying; CSB evaluates them with explicit shortcut controls; and internalization is judged by whether gains persist after clues are removed. After SFT, no-clue capped mean mpWER on overlap plus noise falls from 25 % 25\% – 71 % 71\% to 9 % 9\% – 15 % 15\% , providing operational evidence of internalization. For streaming, gate-only GDPO learns whether and when to use a clue; full-chain GDPO jointly trains the gate and speaker-attributed transcript. Future work will extend scene-matched clues to new scene types and test the learned gate under domain shift. The deeper principle is simple: context should scaffold perception, not replace it.
